question: What is the meaning of maintenance in relation to durability and extended lifetime?
description: Maintenance in relation to durability and extended lifetime refers to the activities and processes carried out to preserve the functionality, performance, and structural integrity of a product over time. This includes regular inspections, repairs, adjustments, and replacements of worn-out or damaged components to ensure the product continues to operate as intended. By conducting maintenance, the durability of the product is enhanced, and its useful life is extended, thereby reducing the need for frequent replacements and minimizing waste generation. Maintenance plays a crucial role in achieving sustainable construction practices by promoting resource-effectiveness and resource-efficiency, ultimately contributing to the circular economy.

2.2.2. Service providers
From a circularity perspective, service providers have traditionally
been responsible for prolonging product lifetimes through various
maintenance and repair strategies, such as using spare parts to ex-
change defective components. Time-based maintenance has long been
considered the most suitable strategy (Takata et al., 2004). However,
with the purpose of providing more accurate service offers, condition-
based maintenance has gained traction, according to which decisions
are based on data from monitoring product conditions (Ahmad and
Kamaruddin, 2012). Although such a change of approach is not a new
phenomenon and was hardly sparked by the circular transition, it
draws upon the distinction between resource-effectiveness and
resource-efﬁciency that is frequently highlighted in the circular econ-
omy discourse. For instance, Bockholt et al. (2020) argue that
resource-effectiveness is tied to the utilisation of residual value
(e.g., by recovering functional or material value), while resource-
efﬁciency refers to the incremental process improvements of such
activities.
2.2.3. Manufacturers
Due to resource-intensive upstream activities, resource scarcity and
increased focus on extended producer responsibility, manufacturing
companies can no longer be solely concerned with a forward-oriented
supply chain and logistics setup (Lüdeke-Freund et al., 2019). Instead,
they must begin to decouple the consumption of virgin materials from
business growth. In terms of closing resource loops, one essential mea-
sure relates to the development of product take-back systems, as well as
capabilities to retain value at its highest utility (Geissdoerfer et al.,
2017). Consequently, manufacturers must be able to select and employ
suitable value-retention strategies at product level – assessing potential
for products to be reused or remanufactured, or whether selected com-
ponents or materials can be returned to suppliers or third-party
recycling companies (Lopes de Sousa Jabbour et al., 2019).
2.2.4. Suppliers
Rather than solely seeking material input from virgin resources, sup-
pliers can improve sustainable value creation by developing capabilities
to remanufacture post-market components (Xiong et al., 2016). The ad-
vantages of doing so include the utilisation of material expertise and
existing facilities. In the early stages of circular transition, suppliers
may ﬁnd remanufacturing less attractive than manufacturers. However,
as manufacturers increasingly explore remanufacturing, suppliers be-
come incentivised to follow suit, as they would ﬁnancially beneﬁt
from remanufacturing their post-market components over the alterna-
tive scenario, in which manufacturers would remanufacture the sup-
pliers' components and thus reduce revenue for the supplier (Huang
and Wang, 2017).
2.2.5. Third-party recycling companies
Although some manufacturers and suppliers have facilities to recycle
materials (e.g., to remelt aluminium), many have outsourced this
activity to third-party recycling companies. As opposed to the other ac-
tors, recycling companies are born with a circular purpose, albeit one
that is seen as a ‘last resort’ since only the material value is left to be
retained (Bockholt et al., 2020). Nevertheless, recycling companies are
also ﬁnding themselves in transition. Traditionally, the common under-
standing has been that ‘all recycling is good recycling’. As such, these
companies have been measured on the amounts of materials sent to
recycling or the recovery rate (Graedel et al., 2011). Now, increasing at-
tention is directed towards the utilisation and quality of recycling mate-
rials, and recycling companies are being encouraged to prepare
materials for the highest utility on the market, thus conducting
recycling with reversible loss of material properties whenever appropri-
ate.
In sum, a variety of actors ﬁnd themselves transitioning towards new
roles. Although they are listed as having distinct intraorganisational re-
sponsibilities, signiﬁcant value is to be found in interorganisational collab-
oration and increased exchange of data and information (Leising et al.,
2018).

3.3. Proposed framework to enable dynamic information flow
The literature review indicates that current DPP development lacks
focus on updating information during the maintenance phase by third-
party service providers. To address this gap, we propose a blockchain-
based DPP system design that facilitates dynamic information flow
and ensures secure and effective updates, particularly for maintenance
information provided by third-party service providers during the prod-
uct use phase. Given the limited emphasis in the literature on post-
launch data inclusion mechanisms, our proposal highlights the impor-
tance of incorporating user verification and authorization within the
blockchain-based DPP system.
Based on the findings in Section 4, the core requirements for this
framework include data source, data carrier, data security, and user
access and verification. Since the data source involves third-party ser-
vice providers, a blockchain-based DPP is suitable to enhance data se-
curity and trust in data sharing, as it has been widely adopted in DPP

3.3.1. Framework explanation
To address the data collection of maintenance service by 3rd party
service provider during the launch of the product of DPP, we proposed
conceptual framework consists of several key components such as the
DPP and user management illustrated in. Our framework enables the
updating of maintenance history (e.g. condition-based maintenance/
repair) by 3rd party service provider. This information is important for
recyclers/manufacturers to understand recycling or circularity potential
and support decisions making at the end of life of a product.
The DPP should use a unique identifier so that all data generated
throughout the product life cycle can be associated with it. ID man-
agement is a central aspect of DPP management. When a DPP is created,
a unique ID (e.g., a URL) will be assigned to the DPP to ensure that the
DPP can be updated and accessible throughout all the product life cycle
phases. We propose the use of standards, such as GS-1 Digital Link (GS1,
2023), to ensure globally identifiable, unique IDs. This is crucial for data
consistency in a decentralized system. In addition, a product tag that
contains a data carrier such as QR codes or RFIDs will be used to link
physical products with their DPPs. A scanning app (e.g., a mobile QR
code reader) can then be used to retrieve and update the DPP data.
A key component in our framework is the role of blockchain tech-
nology. Blockchain can provide an immutable record of events, ensuring
that every update, transaction, or change is recorded in chronological
order.
